segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yousef has been moving and convincing his sisters to move since the war began. They all started the war in Jabalia, in the northern part of Gaza. After October 7, when Hamas attacked southern Israel and killed around 1,200 people, took about 240 people hostage, Yousef immediately moved his family from Jabalia to his parents' house in a nearby city, Beit Lahiya. They moved the very next day, October 8.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: On October 9, Israeli airstrikes hit Jabalia, and then again on October 12, 19, 22, 31, November 1, 2, 4, and on. Yousef and his family and his sisters' families then fled south to Khan Yunis. They stayed with relatives until Yousef read a leaflet that fell from the sky. It said, you must evacuate immediately and go to shelters in the city of Rafah. The city of Khan Yunis is a dangerous combat zone. Forewarned is forearmed. It was signed the Israeli Defense Forces.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's when he fled to Rafah with his wife and his kids. By that point in the war, over 15,000 people in Gaza had been killed. The place Yousef works, the NRC, had rented an office in Rafah, in the area the Israelis were now saying was a safe zone. Yousef moved his immediate family into the office, but his sisters and their families weren't so sure they wanted to follow this time. So Yousef, from the moment he got to Rafah, had been pushing his sisters in Khan Yunis to come. He'd been at that for almost a week.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: To be honest, each one of them have its own personality, and I have to persuade her the way I know. Each one of them. segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash

segments.text: Wow, you did it. Took you--

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Oof, it was really a lot. [LAUGHS] Last night, they were texting me about a lot of bombing. The house next to them was bombed. Another house behind them was bombed. And so they wanted to move. They wanted to go at last.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yousef, the house next to them was bombed last night?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yes. Yeah, last night was a bit harsh when they started texting me that the bombing is around us. What?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah. But there was an airstrike that hit a property right next to them.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yes, but it's a drone strike. So, OK, we have different types of missiles that the Israelis are using. So there is the F-16, which is warplanes and this American-made weapon that are destroying entire neighborhoods. The drones have smaller bombs that destroy a house or half of the house. They were afraid that the bombing might be in the same house because it's four floors, and they are on the first one. So that's why they didn't argue me and like, yes, let's move.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you think about going in the night?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, I told them I'm coming.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You texted back, I'm coming?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yes, and they were freaking out that I will come. And my wife prevented me. My sisters were texting me, do not come. There is a lot of bombing in the street in front of the house. Do not come.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yousef waited till the sun came up and then drove to Khan Yunis. He says on his way there, he could hear gunfire and explosions all around him.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: The first thing I did in the morning is, I went there, pack up in the car my sisters and their children. And then I came, and then I sent another car, like a small van, small bus, so I can have the bags and everything and my brothers-in-law.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Was there a part of you that felt a little frustrated, like I told you guys you should have come earlier? I didn't want it to get to this.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: That's exactly the first thing I said today when I met them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [LAUGHS] That was how you greeted them?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What did you say?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: And the first thing was like, I told you. 'Cause it was a lot of bombing, a lot of tanks. Like, I told you before. We don't need to run away under shelling and bombing. But now we did it. Khalas. Every time it had to be the same situation.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So, overnight, you're worried about their survival, and you're panicked, and you want to drive to get them in the middle of the night. But in the morning, you greet them with, "I told you so." This is what I said was going to happen.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah. I was blaming them. So there is no discussion. We are leaving.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So you didn't like hug them and cry and say, I'm so glad you survived. You said, get in the car.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: No, no, we have a different type of relation. It's not about hugging them. I was laughing. You should have died. I should be in the morgue now. [CHUCKLES] This is how I am with my sisters.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And did they laugh? What did they say?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Hadir was like, ah, you know. Actually, they will start to give me orders quickly. You need to talk to our cousin, Amajid, because he was hosting us. You need to invite him. You have to talk to him nicely and push to bring them with us because they take care of us for a long time. Now we have to repay them.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Also, go to our Uncle Ayman because they wanted to have invited by you, not us. It's a bit weird. Like, OK, I'll do this. And you pack the luggage, and you do that. And they refused to leave before cleaning everything.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They wouldn't leave without cleaning the house?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yep, cleaning the house, kitchen, bathrooms,

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Even though you're fleeing bombing?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yes, because they will-- yeah, yeah, that was actually weird from them. But this is how they think, and I really respect it because we leave it better than the way we have. This is how we show respect. And we had to clean.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And then you left.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Then we left.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What did it--

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: And so it was the first time for them since the beginning of the war to see the sea.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: And they were very, very excited and happy.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How did they respond to the tents when you showed them where they're staying?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: I was expecting that they will be like, ah, it's not nice. It's whatever. But they were happy. It's like, OK, it's nice. It's good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you feel nervous?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. I want them to see that-- to prove for them that I did my best. And I was checking on them inside the tents. What do you think? It's warm. There is two layers for the tent, one for if it's rain and one inside. I was trying to convince them as you know these sale people who is trying to convince you to buy something?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Uh-huh. That was you?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: That's exactly what I was. That was me today. Yeah, no, it's nice. Good. We'll do with the bathroom here. We'll get something there. Here, we can turn on the fire. And I was like, oh, well, maybe I'll get you internet tomorrow. And I will get you lights here. Our neighbors have a solar panel. He will connect us some lights. Yeah, I was trying-- I was doing that salesman. And they were happy.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They were? Did they give you the response you wanted?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, it's like, yeah, it's nice. Also, in our way coming, we went through one of the camps that people are just building tents in the streets. And they saw how miserable the situation is. And I meant to go there before taking them to our place.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You did it on purpose?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Exactly, because I want them to see how people are living to prove for them that I did my best, managing what I could. When I met them today, I found out that they didn't eat for two days. They only eat rice. So first thing I was thinking about preparing a really big meal for them, and they were surprised. I had barbecues and kebab. And I was like, no, no, no.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So they had a meal? You had a meal together?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: A very big one. It was very expensive one, but I was like, OK, I'll feed you until you've had more than enough. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: And so, after fasting for two days, it was to provide them with something really good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did they appreciate it?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Ooh, a lot. They were very happy. I was very happy also, having this meal.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The next day, Yousef went to work, his family getting settled right nearby. He made it a couple hours into the day when he got a call from his youngest sister, Aseel.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: It's too complicated.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wait, tell me what happened with your sister.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: So Aseel today wanted to go to the bathroom, and she waited. So there is in the land next to us, they have a bathroom and they are friends of mine. And my neighbor is hosting more than 60 people. So they have to wait in line to earn this bathroom. It's a single bathroom.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: [SIGHS] Well, yes, and she cannot wait. She is pregnant and ya'ani. It's a bit embarrassing for her. And so she started to cry, and then she called me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: While she was in line?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: So she tried several times, and she was hopeless. Then she started to cry and decided to go back to Khan Yunis.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [GASPS]

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: She decided that, and she called me and she told me, I am leaving to Khan Yunis now. Oh, that changed the day. I had to go back to meet my sister, take her to the bathroom, spend an hour or more. I stopped the line.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How did the 60 people waiting respond to that?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Ah, it went OK. I told them no one is getting inside. No one goes to the bathroom, hallas, until my sister finished.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Was she seriously thinking about going back to Khan Yunis?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: I don't think so. It shows me that she needs me. I need to find a solution now. She's above the limit.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How pregnant is she? When is she due?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: That's another alarming thing. So she is at the seventh month, about to finish it. So I guess she is going [SIGHS] through a lot.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The whole week, Yousef had been telling me he needed his family close to him. Now, they're here. They're together in Rafah. They'd moved from the very north of Gaza all the way down, at the bottom edge of the Gaza Strip on the border with Egypt. Yousef was now responsible for his own camp of about 60 people, one of whom was eight months pregnant, and all of whom were looking to him to tell them, what now? What's the plan?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Chana Joffe-Walt. Coming up, things do not go like Yousef planned. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today, we're telling the story of Yousef Hammash. He spent months moving his family from one place to another in Gaza, trying to keep them safe. Until, finally, at the end of last year, he got them out of Rafah, an enormous feat that-- I don't want to idealize Yousef here, but there are few people who have the special combination of resources and familial relationships and trust and also skills and planning abilities and really luck to pull off what Yousef just pulled off-- getting 60 people to Rafah housed and together and seemingly, for the moment, safe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So, by the beginning of this year, they're all settled in Rafah, waiting. But every day, there's talk that Israel is going to launch a ground assault in Rafah next. And Aseel, Yousef's youngest sister, is about to give birth. Again, here's Chana.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I really wanted to talk to Yousef's sister, Aseel. Once he got them all to Rafah, she was the one Yousef was thinking about the most, talked about the most. The funny sister, the emotional sister. Also the one most like Yousef-- resourceful, determined. Yousef told me once Aseel settled in Rafah, she quickly started taking things into her own hands.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: First of all, the tents Yousef built, they were too crowded and loud. Aseel built her own tent with her husband. Every time Yousef went to visit the camp, he'd find everyone in Aseel's tent, hanging out. She began to rebuild other parts of her life there, too. Aseel is a nurse. People in the camp began bringing her their medical questions. She'd advise, follow up, try to source medications for them when she could. Aseel's tent became part living room, part clinic.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yousef had always told me Aseel was his youngest and most stubborn sister. But when she arrived in Rafah, he added, she's also the least fazed. Difficult things do not rattle Aseel, which is why the moment she'd called him, crying in line to the bathroom, was so alarming to him.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, she usually doesn't complain. She doesn't complain. Usually, Aseel is the most-- between my sister, I look to Aseel as the most wise. She's young, but she's expert. She's in love with nursing and all of this. She reads a lot. I spoke a lot about Aseel. And trust me, you'll be surprised when you talk to her.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It was really hard to reach Aseel.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, Aseel. This is Chana.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Hi finally.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, finally the famous sister.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The internet is OK now?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Erm, yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK. Did I lose you?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It was not OK.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: The internet is really bad. Uh, one minute, please.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK, OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The was no internet at the tents and hardly any cell connection. I'd try catch Aseel on the internet at Yousef's office or on her phone.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Hi, Chana.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi. Can you hear me?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: We will try.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK, OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I learned things in scraps of conversation that were maybe two or three minutes long, some voice memos, text messages. Just as Aseel had managed her situation at the camp, she took control of her plans for childbirth, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Aseel told me she'd never been fearful of childbirth. She'd seen lots of births as a nurse. She was actually working in labor and delivery in Gaza City when the war started. She'd imagined it. She could do it. She said, when it comes to health care matters, I'm capable of controlling the situation for myself and those around me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When she had to flee her home, leave behind the doctor she loved and the hospital she had planned to deliver in, Aseel just made a new plan. She found a new hospital and a new doctor in Khan Yunis. When that fell apart and she fled to Rafah, Aseel brought Yousef into her planning process.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In Rafah, Aseel and Yousef worked in tandem. They figured out where she could deliver-- a small maternity hospital. They mapped out a route to the hospital. Rafah is so packed with traffic and people now, it can take hours to get across the city, so Yousef studied routes and Google Maps. And he practiced driving to the hospital on back streets through farmland and bumpy dirt roads.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Aseel didn't want to bring a newborn back to the tent in the cold, so Yousef asked the NRC if Aseel and the baby could stay with him and the other staff living at the NRC office, just for a bit after the birth. They said yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At the camp, they got the bathroom up and running four days after Aseel arrived. By late January, Yousef and Aseel had a bathroom, a route to the hospital, and a postpartum plan. There was only one thing Aseel desperately wanted that she couldn't make happen herself. She told me in Arabic, when we were finally able to talk for a longer stretch.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I've always prayed that I won't give birth until there's a truce. I don't want to start experiencing labor pain before there's a truce. God willing, it will happen.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Every day, there were small glimmers of a possible truce. Negotiations were underway for a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas. It was the last week of January. Aseel was due February 4. With or without a truce, Aseel and Yousef had a plan.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Then, five days before her due date, they had an unexpected dry run that tested their plan. Aseel had contractions in the middle of the night. Yousef raced her to the hospital. It was a false alarm. The contractions subsided. But for the first time, Aseel got to see what it looked like inside the hospital.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: When you enter the hospital, there's an unimaginable number of displaced people. It's full of displaced people. When we were standing at the door, there was a woman coming from Abasan in Khan Yunis. They were displaced, and she came to the hospital in labor. Her water had already broken. She was standing at the door, waiting in line, because there are five or six beds inside, and they are all full. She was waiting for her turn to get examined, even though she couldn't stand. The baby came out while she was waiting at the door.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You saw her give birth, Aseel?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Yeah. The baby is all--

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Yeah, the baby is all-- the baby came out, and they laid her down on the floor to deliver the baby right there. There were no beds, not even in the maternity ward. They laid her down on the floor, and the midwife or the doctor came to deliver the baby with her on the ground.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, wow. In front of you.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Yeah, I feared that I would be in her place. I imagined myself in her place, waiting for my turn to go in for labor, but then for it to happen at the door.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That night, in the hospital, everything suddenly felt very real to Aseel. She was about to give birth in a tiny hospital that used to have around 20 births a day, and now sometimes had 100. She would be delivering her first baby in a city that had 200,000 people just a few months ago and now had 1.5 million.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She was about to give birth in a hospital in the middle of a war that had killed 600 people inside medical facilities and obliterated the vast majority of health care services. She was about to have a child in a war where more than 10,000 children have been killed so far.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Aseel couldn't get unpregnant. She could pray for a ceasefire, but she couldn't wait for one. Aseel had imagined her birth so clearly before the war. But now she was imagining it in ways she never had before. What if she delivered at the hospital on the floor? What if she delivered in her tent alone? What if Israeli tanks came into Rafah while she was in labor? What if she was naked, pushing a baby out, when an Israeli soldier showed up at the door to her tent?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Thinking about this by itself plants terror in my heart. That I could give birth and see the soldiers. The mere sight of the soldiers scares me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And what if after she delivered her baby, she started bleeding? One horrifying thing Aseel knew was happening in Gaza right now is women who hemorrhage after birth are sometimes being given hysterectomies. I've talked to doctors and a midwife in Gaza who told me this is happening. It's happening for lots of reasons.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hospitals don't have the routine medications that help stop bleeding after birth. They also don't have staff. The staff they do have don't have time. Pregnant women are coming in malnourished, sometimes with injuries and other complications. And they're going into labor severely anemic. So, if they hemorrhage after birth, which happens sometimes, things quickly become life threatening. They're using hysterectomies in Gaza because hysterectomies can be the fastest and safest way to save lives.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Of all the very real possibilities Aseel was now imagining, this was the one she feared the most. She'd deliver her baby, start bleeding, and they'd take her uterus. That night in the hospital, she begged a doctor for his attention. Is it safe here? I'm a medical professional, she said. Please help me. The doctor told her, if you can deliver somewhere else, you should. Aseel walked out of the hospital to the car where Yousef was waiting and told him, I cannot have my baby here.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: I could see it in her eyes today. I don't think I have the capacity to translate into English what she was saying, but it's related to medical stuff that he saw with other females there. So I was like, no, I'll find a solution. Tomorrow, I'll figure it out.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yousef began calling people he knew, asking about other options for delivering a baby in Rafah, maybe a private doctor who could deliver outside the hospital. But those conversations quickly became other conversations. His coworkers, friends, said, but Yousef, are you seeing this? Did you see what Yoav Gallant just said, the Israeli Defense minister? He's saying Rafah is next.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Gallant, Yoav Gallant, who said that when we finish from Khan Yunis, we will go into Rafah. And that's a huge concern. For example, from where I am staying, the Israeli tanks in Al-Aqsa University, it's less than 1 kilometer. I can hear the tanks moving clearly. I can hear the clashes clearly. And I think if the Israelis decided to continue the ground operation in Rafah, it's going to take them three minutes to arrive me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When Yousef thinks of those three minutes, he's not just thinking of himself. He's thinking of the 60 people he moved from other parts of Gaza to here. He's thinking how he promised this was the safest place to be.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Building that camp, hosting these families, and then if the Israelis decided to start the ground operation in Rafah, it's going to be like an ambush. It's going to be like, I create an ambush for these families, bringing families to live in that place, and the Israelis killing. I don't know, you know.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's going to be on you.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yes, at least I will feel it on me. Also, their relatives, their father-in-laws, all of them I'm hosting them in the camp I build. So I'm also responsible, at least, to inform these families that it's not safe here. I remember what happened in Khan Yunis also. And they would start talking about Khan Yunis, and they destroyed the entire city.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I know. I can't believe you're in this situation again. This is exactly where you were when we talked--

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: --in early December.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: [SIGHS] Now that's a long time. That's a long time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Are you thinking about moving again?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: I'll have to think about the options that I have, yeah, if we are going. And I was thinking about Deir al Balah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why Deir al Balah? Why was that a place that you looked at?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: This is the only areas that considered safe by the Israelis. They said either Rafah or Deir al Balah. But today I was looking for the statistics of Deir al Balah. On a daily basis, there is at least five targeted, five houses targeted in Deir al Balah. So I have to think more twice about that. You cannot make a decision because nothing is clear.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah. And did you find a doctor for Aseel?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Uh, yes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wow, you found a doctor already?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Is it incredibly expensive?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: She found it. We didn't agree yet, but I told him I'll pay whatever you want. I just want her to be safe and in an appropriate place and all of that. So I don't care about financial things.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: February 3, the day before her due date, Yousef, the private doctor, and Aseel agreed on a new plan. She would deliver at a clinic outside the hospital. The doctor promised they were equipped to deal with complications there without doing a hysterectomy. Five days later, February 8, still no baby.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: February 9, the prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, ordered the military to develop a plan to evacuate Rafah, to clear the way for a ground assault on Rafah. That same day, I got a message from Yousef. Aseel is currently in the hospital for the birth. I called several hours later. Yousef was outside the hospital, waiting. Aseel was inside with his wife and their mom. He told me the baby had arrived. She was healthy. But he wasn't sure about his sister.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: But Aseel, she's still under watch inside. So, unfortunately, she was bleeding, so we are waiting.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She's bleeding?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: She did a natural birth, but I think she had an issue, and she was bleeding. The doctors, all the doctors at the hospital were running, trying to control it. So it was-- I couldn't get inside because I will see through a small window that there are so many doctors around. And it's like, what's going on there? And he told me that she's bleeding, and they're trying to control it. And then after that, he informed me that they control it, but they have to wait a bit. Ah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Where is her-- was her husband there?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, her husband is very young, so that's why I have to be there, even, to ask for everything because Aseel was like, I want Yousef here, right? My mother and so many women are screaming around. And I cannot keep hearing her screaming. That's why I had to go out. I have to leave.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, Aseel.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Hi, Chana.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, Mabrouk.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Hello. [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How are you doing?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A week after she gave birth, I reached Aseel in Yousef's office. She was in bed with her mom and her new baby. She was incredibly weak. And she could not walk. Instead of the careful plan Aseel and Yousef made, she told me something very different happened. Her water broke in the middle of the night. They couldn't reach the private doctor. And Yousef couldn't get to Aseel quickly enough to drive her.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So a friend took her to exactly the place she didn't want to go-- the hospital. When she got there, she waited in the hallway, just as she feared, 12 hours in labor. She was begging for a room, a bed, for someone to help her.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: There was no room for me. There was no anesthetics, no nothing. I couldn't stand. I couldn't sit. I couldn't do anything. My sister spoke with the nurse there, and she told her I couldn't stand in line, and that I was about to give birth.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: There was no chair for you to sit on?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: No, no, there was no chairs at all. There was only the doctor's chair. And I took it from her.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Aseel sat in the hallway on the stolen chair for more hours, more contractions. She felt the baby's head, the need to push. Finally, they called her back, rushed her to a bed. But Aseel looked at the bed and froze.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: The bed sheet on it was the same one the woman before me gave birth on. It was covered in blood. So I took it off and told them to get the cleaner to wipe the bed.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: While you were in labor?

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Yes, yes. I couldn't sit in the bed, even with my pain. I'm willing to endure the pain a bit, but in a clean place and deliver the baby in a clean, sanitized place.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In bed, Aseel immediately had to push. She pushed, feeling utter panic, pushed and pushed without stopping, without breaks. She had an internal hemorrhage. The doctor made an incision to make the opening bigger. She bled more. The whole day, Aseel had been directing the people around her for a chair, for a clean sheet. But once the baby arrived, she lost control. The nurses took the baby. Then Aseel hemorrhaged for three hours, while doctors tried to stop the bleeding.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Five doctors came in. I couldn't stay with them. I couldn't keep my eyes open. After about an hour of stitching and 28 stitches-- there was no anesthesia or anything-- I was appealing to God, 28 stitches between internal and external. I couldn't speak back to them or tell them I couldn't-- that I was dizzy. I couldn't speak to them at all. I had surrendered to the pain. He told me that if it didn't work, they'll be forced to do a hysterectomy. I kept quiet and prayed that it wouldn't happen.

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I wasn't present, but I felt the thread going in. I felt the prick of the needle. I was crying a lot and praying to God that it would be the last stitch. Every time I prayed it would be the last stitch, they told me there was one more. You're almost there. This is the last one. I couldn't wait to leave the room. I couldn't move. And I was calling for my brother, saying, I can't do it, and for someone to get me out.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You were calling for Yousef?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Because he would try to control the bad things that happen to us. For me, it was like, you can help me in this matter, too. Come save me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Eventually, the doctors finished the stitches and gave Aseel a blood transfusion. An obstetrician practicing in Gaza told me Aseel was very lucky the hospital had blood that day. All the donated blood is from within Gaza, and most days, there's not enough. Aseel lost so much blood, she couldn't see clearly. Normally, after hemorrhaging that much, you'd stay in the hospital for a few days. It's hard to move. You're weak, in pain. There's danger of infection, fainting. She had the stitches. But Aseel was desperate to get out of there.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: They told me not to leave because I couldn't get up. The stitches hurt a lot. I told them I wanted to leave because the place is not clean and because the displaced go there, so you can't get rest. Yousef came to the hospital entrance. I couldn't get myself there, so I used a chair. They didn't have a wheelchair, so I used a normal chair for support. And I walked. I took the elevator down to the car.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You had to get yourself to the elevator with the help of a chair?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Yes. I used the chair to get to the elevator. And when I got down, there's a 10-meter-long hallway or something like that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, my God.

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: And so I used the chair for support until I got to the car. Yousef then carried me into the car. He carried me and put me inside the car.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I didn't even pay attention to the baby's features until I got a blood transfusion and started to feel better.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What did she look like when you were able to see her?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: When I first saw her, I said she looked a lot like Yousef and his little son.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, really? Ahmed?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you feel happy about that?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, it was one of the longest days of my life.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That picture is so beautiful of you with the baby.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah. When I take it, I was happy and excited. Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You look much skinnier. I hope it's OK to say that.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, I lost so much weight, you know. Canned food.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, that's fine.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yousef said, holding the baby, he felt immense relief.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, it reduced all that pressure that I was having for a couple of months about that moment. And finally, I reach it. It was a glimmer of hope. And I was waiting to have that feeling, all of that period, all that pressure in my head every day about Aseel's pregnancy, when she's going to do the birth, where, blah, blah, blah, all of that is over.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: He got Aseel and the baby home from the hospital, or at least, to the office that is now home, where he'd created a bed for them to share with his mom. Everyone went to sleep. That night, at 1:00 in the morning, Yousef woke up to bombing. It was louder and brighter than anything he'd experienced in Rafah before. It felt like it was right nearby, inside Rafah.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: The house was shaking, huge bombardment. There's children screaming. And I thought that the Israelis, they start the operation, and I will find the tanks in front of my place. And that's it. I was going to-- I was about to put on my underwear because this is the way they take us men, wearing only underwear.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wait, why were you going to put on your underwear?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: No, so, actually, I was joking, but usually, the Israelis, when they collect men, whenever they go on the ground and they collect men above 16 years old, wearing only underwear.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You mean they make them take off their clothes?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, that's a dark thought to have in the middle of the night.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Actually, I was joking. I was telling Manal, my wife, I need to prepare the underwear. It should be warm. This is part of our life experience, so sorry. Yeah, it's kind of a joke. I know it's a dark humor, but that's me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What did your wife say?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: It wasn't actually the right moment to make jokes. I don't usually find the right timing for to make jokes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Manal was not appreciating your joke at that moment?

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: No. No. Yeah, we had to collect the kids between us and trying to warm them and to calm them. And so we tried to get them back to sleep, but-- because nothing we can do more than that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In the morning, Yousef was finally able to get online and figure out what just happened the night before. That night, Israel rescued two Israeli hostages from Rafah, two older men who'd been held captive for months since October 7.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And Israel killed, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, at least 94 Palestinians. Amnesty International says half the people killed in Rafah that night were children, including a two-week-old baby girl. That was Aseel's first night out of the hospital, in bed with her mom next to her, praying through six hours of bombing and the baby crying.

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I couldn't move or anything. I was scared. I waited for Yousef to come down in the morning and asked him if there's going to be a ground invasion in Rafah because I couldn't walk. I couldn't carry the baby and stand.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah. What did he say?

segments.speaker: Aseel
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: He said, don't worry. That won't happen. I told him all I was worried about happened. Waiting in line in the hospital happened. The difficult labor happened. And now they are entering here? No, at least this one shouldn't happen.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Are you starting to doubt his reassurances when he says, don't worry?

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: No, for me, what he says is what happens. I believe him.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Right now, there are dozens of people waiting to see what Yousef says, what he's lining up for them next. He's launched into overdrive, calling friends, colleagues, carefully parsing official statements on a possible Rafah invasion, and looking for a place they could flee to, a building that's still standing, a piece of land he can rent and build tents-- exactly what he was doing when I first called him back in early December. Only now, he's exhausted. He's skinnier. His sister just had a baby and can't walk. Yousef has been quite ill several times. And 30,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war started.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And it's not over. Right now, for the first time since Yousef began moving his family on October 8 to keep them safe, Yousef is not finding options. This time, there really may not be anywhere to go.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Actually, to be honest, I don't want to think about that because I know there is no solution. And it's going to be just a headache to go through details, what I will do. What-- Aseel, what about Habil, what about Heba, what about Salsabeel, what about my wife and the children, my mother. And it's responsibility above responsibility. And unfortunately, this time, I'm completely useless because I ran out of options. And when I think about it deeply, there is no solution. There is no option ahead of me. So what am I going to do?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I have never heard you talk like that, Yousef. I've never heard you say that. You're always the guy that's like, yeah, I'll figure it out. I'll call so-and-so tomorrow. Or no, we don't have it right now, but I'll figure it out.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: I don't have enough resources to manage this now. It's chaotic situation. And I don't think I'm mentally stable to take a decision now. I'm trying to avoid thinking about it because I'm not prepared because I don't have solutions. I don't have options ahead of me. When I have options, I'll start to think deeply about it. But up to now, I'm completely useless.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: I'm calling my friends who are, ya'ani, scattered everywhere in Gaza. And they just keep searching, but I cannot find. My friend called me several times, actually. So I need to talk to him. Maybe I can call you back after?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Sure, sure.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Yeah, OK, just I will try to get some news from him.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: OK. Thank you, Chana. Thank you. OK.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Bye. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Yousef Hammash
segments.text: Bye, bye, bye.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
